# Outliers, Leverage, and Influence {#sec-regression-diagnostics}

A fitted regression line summarizes the observations, but some observations may matter much more than others. We ask three different questions: **is the response unusual given the predictors, are the predictor values unusual, and does the observation substantially change the fit?** These lead to outliers, leverage, and influence. We use the same small dataset throughout so that every diagnostic can be connected to a visible change in the estimates.

> **Learning Objectives**
>
> By the end of this chapter, students should be able to:
>
> - distinguish a response outlier, a high-leverage observation, and an influential observation;
> - compare coefficient estimates and predictions with and without one observation;
> - interpret leverage, standardized residuals, and externally studentized residuals;
> - explain how Cook's distance combines response discrepancy and predictor position;
> - investigate a flagged observation and report a sensitivity analysis.

::: {#ch6-prerequisite-recap .callout-note title="Quick Recap: What We Will Use"}

- **Mean model and design — [Chapter 1](01_matrix_representation.qmd#the-linear-regression-model).** Write $\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, with $\mathbb E(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\mathbf0$. A row describes an observation; a column multiplies a coefficient. Let $p$ count the columns, including the intercept. We assume full column rank and $n>p$.
- **Fitted values and residuals — [Chapter 2](02_LSE.qmd#the-hat-matrix).** OLS gives $\hat{\mathbf Y}=\mathbf H\mathbf Y$ and $\mathbf e=(\mathbf I-\mathbf H)\mathbf Y$, where $\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top$. A residual is an observed deviation from the fitted mean, not the unobserved error.
- **Noise and uncertainty — [Chapter 3](03_OLS_inference.qmd#def-mse).** Under $\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2\mathbf I$, estimate $\sigma^2$ by $s^2=\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p)$. Here $\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i e_i^2$ is the unexplained variation from [Chapter 4](04.qmd#def-regression-sums-of-squares). Estimated coefficient covariance is $s^2(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}$.
- **Interpret the quantity that changes — [Chapter 5](05.qmd#sec-ch5-adjusted).** An additive slope describes a mean-response difference holding other predictors fixed. To assess influence, compare the coefficients and predictions relevant to that question, using the same model specification.

:::

## See how one observation changes the fit {#sec-ch6-influence}

First look at the data and the fitted lines. We will name the three concepts after seeing how they differ, then introduce their numerical measures.

::: {#exm-ch6-three-points}

## Three Points, Three Different Stories

**Look at the lines first.** Every panel starts with the same six green observations, whose fitted line is $\hat y=2+x$. We add **one orange point at a time**. The dashed gray line omits that point; the solid purple line includes it. Compare the point's vertical position, its horizontal position, and how much the line moves.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch6-influence-stories
#| echo: false
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "The same six baseline observations appear in every panel. A shifts the line upward without changing its slope. B lies far to the right but leaves the line unchanged. C is equally far to the right and pulls the line downward, sharply reducing its slope."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels compare a dashed baseline line with a solid line after adding one point. A adds (3.5, 10.5) near the predictor center and shifts the line upward. B adds (10, 12) on the baseline line and the lines coincide. C adds (10, 4), pulling the right side of the line downward."
library(ggplot2)
ch6_base <- data.frame(x = 1:6, y = c(2.8, 4.2, 5, 6, 7.2, 7.8))
ch6_base_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = ch6_base)
ch6_cases <- c("A: response outlier", "B: high leverage", "C: influential point")
ch6_added <- data.frame(x = c(3.5, 10, 10), y = c(10.5, 12, 4))
ch6_story_fits <- vector("list", 3)
ch6_story_data <- ch6_story_lines <- vector("list", 3)
for (j in seq_along(ch6_cases)) {
  d <- rbind(ch6_base, ch6_added[j, ])
  fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
  ch6_story_fits[[j]] <- fit
  d$Case <- ch6_cases[j]
  d$Added <- seq_len(nrow(d)) == nrow(d)
  ch6_story_data[[j]] <- d
  grid <- data.frame(x = seq(0.7, 10.7, length.out = 100))
  ch6_story_lines[[j]] <- rbind(
    data.frame(grid, y = predict(fit, grid), Case = ch6_cases[j],
      Fit = "Including orange point"),
    data.frame(grid, y = predict(ch6_base_fit, grid), Case = ch6_cases[j],
      Fit = "Omitting orange point"))
}
names(ch6_story_fits) <- c("A", "B", "C")
ch6_story_data <- do.call(rbind, ch6_story_data)
ch6_story_lines <- do.call(rbind, ch6_story_lines)
ch6_story_labels <- data.frame(Case = ch6_cases,
  Label = c("Near center in x\nAbove the original line",
    "Far to the right\nOn the original line",
    "Far to the right\nBelow the original line"))
ggplot(ch6_story_data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(data = ch6_story_lines, aes(colour = Fit, linetype = Fit),
    linewidth = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = subset(ch6_story_data, !Added), colour = "#247A6B", size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = subset(ch6_story_data, Added), shape = 21,
    fill = "#E5A14A", colour = "#8A4700", size = 3.2, stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = ch6_story_labels, aes(x = 0.9, y = 13.7, label = Label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 2.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ Case, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Including orange point` = "#593196",
    `Omitting orange point` = "#777777")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`Including orange point` = "solid",
    `Omitting orange point` = "dashed")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.7, 10.7), ylim = c(2, 14)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor x", y = "Response y", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- **A: unusual response, ordinary predictor value.** At $x=3.5$, the original line predicts 5.5, but the orange response is 10.5. This point is near the center of the predictor values and far above the line. It mainly shifts the line upward.
- **B: high leverage without a change in the fitted line.** The new $x=10$ lies beyond the original range of 1 to 6. Its response, 12, lies exactly on the extension of the original line. The point has the potential to pull the fit, but here the two lines coincide.
- **C: high leverage with a large change in the fitted line.** The predictor is again $x=10$, but the response is 4 instead of 12. The point pulls down the right side of the line, substantially reducing the estimated slope.

These descriptions can overlap. C is also a high-leverage point; its **actual effect on the fit** makes it influential. A also affects the fit, even though its effect on the slope differs from C's.

**Now put numbers on the changes.** The six baseline observations are:

```{r}
#| label: ch6-influence-baseline-data
#| echo: false
ch6_baseline_display <- data.frame(Variable = c("x", "y"),
  as.data.frame(rbind(ch6_base$x, ch6_base$y)))
knitr::kable(ch6_baseline_display, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Variable", paste0("Obs. ", 1:6)),
  digits = 1, format.args = list(nsmall = 1), align = "c")
```

Fit `lm(y ~ x)` to the baseline data, then add A, B, or C separately. The table reports the intercept, slope, fitted mean at $x=6$, and residual standard deviation $s$. Removing the orange point from any of the three augmented datasets returns the baseline fit.

```{r}
#| label: ch6-influence-estimate-changes
#| echo: false
ch6_compare_fits <- c(list(Baseline = ch6_base_fit), ch6_story_fits)
ch6_estimate_changes <- t(vapply(ch6_compare_fits, function(m) {
  c(Intercept = unname(coef(m)[1]), Slope = unname(coef(m)[2]),
    Fitted_at_6 = unname(predict(m, newdata = data.frame(x = 6))),
    Residual_SD = sigma(m))
}, numeric(4)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Fit = c("Baseline", "Baseline + A", "Baseline + B", "Baseline + C"),
  ch6_estimate_changes, row.names = NULL),
  digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3), row.names = FALSE, align = "c",
  col.names = c("Fit", "Intercept", "Slope", "Fitted mean at 6", "Residual SD"))
```

- **A changes the intercept and the noise estimate.** The intercept rises from 2.000 to 2.714, while the slope stays at 1.000. Here $x=3.5$ is the baseline mean of $x$, so this added point does not change the slope. The residual SD rises from 0.200 to 2.078: an outlying response can inflate estimated noise even when the slope is unchanged.
- **B leaves both coefficient estimates unchanged.** The fitted mean at $x=6$ remains 8.000. High leverage alone does not imply that a point changes the estimated line; it can still affect the precision of the estimates.
- **C changes the estimated relationship.** The slope falls from 1.000 to 0.170 and the intercept rises to 4.532. The fitted mean at $x=6$ falls from 8.000 to 5.553. This is a substantial change in a prediction within the original predictor range, not just at the distant added point.

:::

These pictures motivate three distinct definitions.

::: {#def-ch6-outlier-leverage-influence}

## Outlier, Leverage, and Influence

- A **response outlier** has an unusual response *given its predictor values and the specified model*. A large volume alone does not make a large tree an outlier.
- A **high-leverage observation** has an unusual configuration of predictor values. Leverage concerns the predictors jointly and does not depend on the observed responses. It measures the potential to pull the fit.
- An **influential observation** changes the fitted coefficients or predictions substantially when omitted. Influence concerns the sensitivity of the analysis, rather than unusualness alone.

:::

## High leverage: unusual predictor values {#sec-ch6-leverage}

Leverage asks **where the observation sits among the predictor rows**. It does not use its response. From the [hat matrix](02_LSE.qmd#the-hat-matrix), define $h_{ii}$ as diagonal entry $i$. With an intercept and one predictor,

$$
h_{ii}=\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2}.
$$

The first term is shared by all observations; the second grows as $x_i$ moves away from the predictor center. The mean and sum in this formula use **all observations in the fit being diagnosed**, including the point of interest. With several predictors, leverage measures unusualness of the whole predictor combination, not just one variable at a time.

```{r}
#| label: ch6-story-diagnostics
#| echo: false
ch6_story_diagnostics <- t(vapply(ch6_story_fits, function(m) {
  c(Leverage = unname(tail(hatvalues(m), 1)),
    Standardized_residual = unname(tail(rstandard(m), 1)),
    Cooks_distance = unname(tail(cooks.distance(m), 1)))
}, numeric(3)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Point = c("A", "B", "C"),
  Added_x = ch6_added$x, Leverage = ch6_story_diagnostics[, "Leverage"]),
  digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3), row.names = FALSE, align = "c",
  col.names = c("Point", "Added x", "Leverage"))
```

For A, $x=3.5$ remains the predictor mean, so its leverage is $1/7=0.143$. B and C have the **same predictor rows**, so both have leverage 0.721 even though their responses are different. B leaves the estimated line unchanged; C changes it substantially. Thus high leverage indicates **potential influence**, not a conclusion that the fit has changed.

Because $\sum_i h_{ii}=p$, average leverage is $p/n$. In this example, $p=2$ and $n=7$, so the average is $2/7=0.286$. Comparing a value with $2p/n$ is a rough screening rule, not a test or a reason to delete an observation. R returns leverages with `hatvalues(fit)`.

A well-measured high-leverage observation can be useful: under an appropriate model it can provide information about the slope. In B, the slope estimate stays at 1.000 while its estimated standard error falls from 0.048 to 0.024. Whether the model is credible at that distant predictor value still needs scientific judgment.

## Outliers: unusual responses given the predictors {#sec-ch6-outliers}

An outlier is unusual **relative to the mean predicted by the specified model**. B has the largest response in the example, 12, yet it lies on the fitted line and has zero residual. A's response is smaller, 10.5, but is far above the expected response near $x=3.5$. Looking only at the distribution of $Y$ would miss this distinction.

**Put residuals on a comparable scale.** From the [residual geometry in Chapter 2](02_LSE.qmd#def-residual-maker-matrix),

$$
\operatorname{Var}(e_i\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii}),
\qquad
r_i=\frac{e_i}{s\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}.
$$

The standardized residual $r_i$ accounts for unequal residual variances; it does not make residuals independent. A high-leverage point can pull the fitted line toward itself and leave a small raw residual, so raw residual size alone can be misleading.

**Keep the point from inflating its own noise estimate.** The externally studentized residual uses the residual standard deviation from the fit without observation $i$:

$$
t_i=\frac{e_i}{s_{(-i)}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}.
$$

The numerator and leverage come from the full fit; only the noise estimate is replaced by $s_{(-i)}$. The deleted fit must be estimable and have positive residual degrees of freedom, $n-p-1>0$. R provides `rstandard(fit)` and `rstudent(fit)`. [R diagnostic documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/influence.measures.html).

```{r}
#| label: ch6-story-residuals
#| echo: false
ch6_residual_comparison <- t(vapply(ch6_story_fits, function(m) {
  c(Residual = unname(tail(residuals(m), 1)),
    Standardized = unname(tail(rstandard(m), 1)),
    Studentized = unname(tail(rstudent(m), 1)))
}, numeric(3)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Point = c("A", "B", "C"),
  ch6_residual_comparison, row.names = NULL),
  digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3), row.names = FALSE, align = "c",
  col.names = c("Point", "Residual", "Standardized", "Externally studentized"))
```

For A and C, the full fit's residual SD is much larger than the baseline value 0.200, as the coefficient table in [Section 6.1](#sec-ch6-influence) showed. Removing either added point returns those six baseline observations and their small noise estimate. This explains the much larger externally studentized residuals. These values flag a response discrepancy under the model; they do not establish a recording error.

A and C have similar absolute standardized residuals, yet C changes the slope much more. **Outlyingness and influence answer different questions.**

## Influence: changes in estimates and Cook's distance {#sec-ch6-cook}

Influence asks **how much the fitted result changes when an observation is omitted**. Compare the same model on the remaining observations: changes in the slope, intercept, or scientifically relevant prediction describe what that observation was doing. Cook's distance summarizes movement of the fitted mean vector using both the residual and leverage.

::: {#def-ch6-cook}

## Cook's Distance

Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(-i)}$ be the OLS estimate after omitting observation $i$, and let $\hat Y_{j(-i)}=\mathbf x_j^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(-i)}$ be its prediction at **each of the original $n$ predictor rows**, including row $i$. Cook's distance is

$$
D_i=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n(\hat Y_j-\hat Y_{j(-i)})^2}{p s^2}
=\frac{e_i^2}{p s^2}\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}
=\frac{r_i^2}{p}\frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}}.
$$

Here $s^2$ comes from the full fit. These formulas apply to ordinary unweighted least squares with full column rank and positive residual degrees of freedom; the deleted fit must also be estimable ($h_{ii}<1$).

:::

**Read the two parts.** The first expression asks how much the *whole fitted mean vector* moves after deletion, measured relative to the noise scale and model size. The last combines response discrepancy ($r_i^2$) with leverage ($h_{ii}/(1-h_{ii})$). Thus the largest residual need not produce the largest Cook's distance. $D_i$ is dimensionless; it is not a p-value. [Cook's original article](https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1977.10489493).

**Apply Cook's distance to the same three points.** In each augmented fit, $n=7$ and $p=2$. The diagnostics for its orange point are:

```{r}
#| label: ch6-influence-diagnostic-values
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(Point = c("A", "B", "C"),
  ch6_story_diagnostics, row.names = NULL),
  digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3), row.names = FALSE, align = "c",
  col.names = c("Point", "Leverage", "Standardized residual", "Cook's distance"))
```

A and C have almost the same absolute standardized residual, but C has much higher leverage and a much larger Cook's distance: 6.395 versus 0.414. B has the same leverage as C, yet its zero residual gives zero Cook's distance. These numbers quantify what the plots and coefficient table already showed: **influence depends on both the response discrepancy and the predictor position**.

::: {#exr-ch6-influence}

## Which Point Moves the Fit More?

In a model with $p=2$, point A has $r_A=3$ and $h_{AA}=0.05$; point B has $r_B=1$ and $h_{BB}=0.50$. Compute their Cook's distances. Which point is more influential by this measure? Does either number establish a data error?

:::

::: {#sol-ch6-influence}

$D_A=(9/2)(0.05/0.95)\approx0.237$, while $D_B=(1/2)(0.50/0.50)=0.50$. B has greater influence despite its smaller standardized residual. Neither value establishes an error or justifies deletion; inspect the observations and the scientific consequences of the changed fit.

:::

## Investigate a flag and report the sensitivity {#sec-ch6-investigate}

A diagnostic flag starts an investigation. It is not an instruction to remove a row.

1. **Check the observation.** Verify units, transcription, measurement conditions, and whether it belongs to the population being studied. Correct a confirmed error from the original record when possible.
2. **Read the three measures together.** Use the residual to assess the response discrepancy, leverage to assess predictor position, and Cook's distance to assess the change in fit.
3. **Refit the same model with and without the point.** Compare the coefficients, uncertainty, and predictions that answer the scientific question. Keep both results available.
4. **Investigate the model as well as the data.** A valid observation may reveal an omitted group, an inadequate mean function, or a different error pattern. Several unusual points can also mask one another in single-case diagnostics.
5. **Report what changes and why.** Explain any exclusion using evidence. If a valid point materially changes the conclusion, report that sensitivity rather than silently choosing the more convenient fit.

::: {.callout-important title="Investigate a flag; do not delete by a cutoff"}

Values such as $|t_i|>2$, $h_{ii}>2p/n$, or $D_i>4/n$ are rough **screening guides**, not universal tests or deletion rules. Check units, transcription, measurement conditions, and omitted structure; a valid unusual observation may be scientifically valuable. Compare fits and relevant predictions with and without a flagged case, and explain any exclusion. Inspect related groups of observations too: several unusual cases can mask one another in single-case diagnostics.

:::

For the small example, a concrete report is: “Adding C changes the estimated slope from 1.000 to 0.170 and the fitted mean at $x=6$ from 8.000 to 5.553. C has high leverage and Cook's distance 6.395. This fit is sensitive to C; whether C should be corrected or excluded requires information about how it was observed.”

## Summary {#sec-ch6-summary}

| Concept | Question | Useful measure | What it does not establish |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Response outlier | Is the response unusual given the predictors and model? | Standardized or externally studentized residual | That the observation has high leverage or must be deleted. |
| High leverage | Is the predictor configuration unusual? | Hat-matrix diagonal $h_{ii}$ | That the observation actually changes the estimated line. |
| Influence | Does omitting the observation change the fitted result? | Coefficient/prediction comparison and Cook's distance | That the observation is a data error. |

Use **all three questions**, then investigate the data and report sensitivity. [Chapter 7](07.qmd) considers how to change the functional form and select model terms when developing a regression model.

## Practice Problems {#sec-ch6-practice}

::: {#exr-ch6-practice}

## Practice: Diagnose and Explain

1. B has a larger response than A but a zero residual. Why is the response value alone insufficient to identify an outlier?
2. Why do B and C have the same leverage but different Cook's distances?
3. In A, the slope is unchanged but the intercept and residual SD increase. Is it correct to say the point has no effect on estimation?
4. A high-leverage point has a small raw residual. Explain why this alone does not establish that it is harmless.
5. A student deletes every point with $D_i>4/n$. State what information and analysis are missing.

:::

::: {#sol-ch6-practice}

1. Outlyingness concerns the response relative to the fitted conditional mean. B lies on the original line; A lies well above it at an ordinary predictor value.
2. Their predictor rows are identical, so leverage is identical. Their responses differ: B leaves the line unchanged, while C moves it substantially.
3. No. A affects the intercept, predictions, and estimated noise even though its position at the predictor mean leaves the slope unchanged.
4. A high-leverage observation can pull the fit toward itself. Examine a scaled residual and compare the fitted result with and without that observation.
5. The cutoff is only a screening guide. Verify the observation, examine the model, compare scientifically relevant estimates and predictions with and without the point, and justify any exclusion using evidence.

:::
